request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The Keplerian ellipse leaves enormous, structured residuals: an RMS of about 75,000 arcsec (about 21 degrees), large time-correlated east-west offsets that grow toward the end of the span, and periodogram peaks near the orbital period. The two half-span ellipse fits share the same period (about 725 days, consistent with a ≈ 1.57 AU if log_a is a natural log) but their perihelion longitudes differ by about 38 degrees per orbit. Steady apsidal precession at fixed period points to a central force that departs from inverse-square, not to noise or a mis-set period. A perturbing planet is less likely as the main cause because the drift looks secular and large. Three central-force candidates follow, with rough initial values estimated from the observed precession assuming it is prograde (the sign is not confirmed by the data shown): Newton plus an inverse-cube term (eps ≈ 0.16 AU); a free power law (n ≈ 2.18, with an apsidal angle of π/sqrt(3-n)); and Yukawa as a physically motivated alternative.

proposals.rationale: One extra parameter produces apsidal precession. 38 degrees per orbit at semi-latus rectum p≈1.5 AU suggests eps≈0.16 AU.
A free exponent gives precession of 2π(1/sqrt(3-n)-1) per orbit. The observed 38 degrees per orbit implies n≈2.18, with C free.
A screened force falls off faster with distance than inverse-square, which also causes precession. This is an alternative one-parameter departure from Newton.
